{"presentation":"A 58-year-old man with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (LVEF 25%) and type 2 diabetes is being started on guideline-directed medical therapy. Which of the following is the recommended first-line approach for blocking the renin-angiotensin system?","differentials":[{"name":"Initiate sacubitril/valsartan (an angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor) in place of an ACE inhibitor or ARB as first-line therapy","confidence":5,"topics":["cardiology","heart failure"]},{"name":"Initiate an ACE inhibitor alone in all patients, adding an ARB only if cough develops","confidence":3,"topics":["cardiology"]},{"name":"Start an ARB together with an ACE inhibitor simultaneously for dual renin-angiotensin system blockade","confidence":2,"topics":["cardiology"]},{"name":"Begin hydralazine and isosorbide dinitrate instead of a renin-angiotensin system inhibitor","confidence":2,"topics":["cardiology"]}],"reason":"The 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA heart failure guideline gives a Class 1 recommendation to ARNI therapy with sacubitril/valsartan in place of an ACE inhibitor or ARB as first-line therapy for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. {"presentation":"A 62-year-old man with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (LVEF 30%) remains symptomatic on maximally tolerated lisinopril, carvedilol, and spironolactone. Which additional drug class now has a Class 1 recommendation to reduce cardiovascular death and heart failure hospitalization?","differentials":[{"name":"A sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin or empagliflozin)","confidence":5,"topics":["cardiology","heart failure"]},{"name":"Intravenous iron supplementation for all patients with heart failure regardless of iron status","confidence":3,"topics":["cardiology"]},{"name":"Ivabradine as the next step in every patient with reduced ejection fraction","confidence":2,"topics":["cardiology"]},{"name":"Long-term digoxin to reduce mortality in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction","confidence":2,"topics":["cardiology"]},{"name":"Routine addition of a loop diuretic at a fixed mortality-reducing dose","confidence":2,"topics":["cardiology"]}],"reason":"The 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA guideline defines four foundational therapy classes for HFrEF - an ARNI (or ACE inhibitor/ARB), a beta-blocker, an MRA, and an SGLT2 inhibitor - each carrying a Class 1 recommendation, and SGLT2 inhibitors are used regardless of diabetes status. {"presentation":"A 60-year-old man presents with crushing chest pain of 20 minutes' duration and a suspected acute coronary syndrome. He has no known allergy to aspirin. Which of the following initial actions is correct?","differentials":[{"name":"Give a single loading dose of 300 mg aspirin as soon as possible","confidence":5,"topics":["cardiology","acute coronary syndromes"]},{"name":"Give 75 mg aspirin once daily as the only antiplatelet measure before hospital arrival","confidence":3,"topics":["cardiology"]},{"name":"Administer routine supplemental oxygen to every patient regardless of oxygen saturation","confidence":2,"topics":["cardiology"]},{"name":"Use the response to glyceryl trinitrate to confirm or exclude the diagnosis","confidence":2,"topics":["cardiology"]}],"reason":"NICE CG95 recommends offering a single 300 mg aspirin loading dose as soon as possible in suspected ACS unless there is clear evidence of allergy; other antiplatelet agents should only be given in hospital. {"presentation":"A 67-year-old man with paroxysmal non-valvular atrial fibrillation on apixaban undergoes percutaneous coronary intervention with drug-eluting stenting for NSTEMI. He has normal renal function and moderate bleeding risk. Which of the following antithrombotic strategies is recommended for up to 12 months?","differentials":[{"name":"Continue the oral anticoagulant with clopidogrel, and without prasugrel or ticagrelor, for up to 12 months","confidence":5,"topics":["cardiology","atrial fibrillation"]},{"name":"Aspirin, clopidogrel, and apixaban as full triple therapy for the entire 12 months","confidence":3,"topics":["cardiology"]},{"name":"Stop apixaban and switch to dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin and ticagrelor","confidence":2,"topics":["cardiology"]},{"name":"Warfarin bridging with aspirin monotherapy after 4 weeks","confidence":2,"topics":["cardiology"]},{"name":"Clopidogrel alone for 12 months without any oral anticoagulant","confidence":2,"topics":["cardiology"]}],"reason":"For patients with an ongoing indication for anticoagulation who have had PCI, NICE NG185 recommends continuing the anticoagulant with clopidogrel for up to 12 months, adjusting the DOAC dose according to bleeding, thromboembolic, and cardiovascular risk. Prasugrel and ticagrelor should not routinely be offered in combination with a needed anticoagulant because of bleeding risk, and long-term triple therapy significantly increases bleeding. Stopping anticoagulation entirely would leave the patient unprotected against AF-related stroke.","diagnoses":["Continue the oral anticoagulant with clopidogrel, and without prasugrel or ticagrelor, for up to 12 months","Aspirin, clopidogrel, and apixaban as full triple therapy for the entire 12 months","Stop apixaban and switch to dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin and ticagrelor","Warfarin bridging with aspirin monotherapy after 4 weeks","Clopidogrel alone for 12 months without any oral anticoagulant"],"references":[{"title":"Acute coronary syndromes - Recommendations","org":"NICE","year":2020,"url":"https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng185/chapter/Recommendations"}]}

{"presentation":"A 71-year-old woman is diagnosed with NSTEMI. After aspirin and antithrombin therapy, formal risk assessment (GRACE) estimates her predicted 6-month mortality at 4.5%. According to NICE NG185, which is the most appropriate revascularisation strategy?","differentials":[{"name":"Consider coronary angiography, with follow-on PCI if indicated, within 72 hours of first admission","confidence":5,"topics":["cardiology","acute coronary syndromes"]},{"name":"Immediate coronary angiography within 2 hours, because all NSTEMI patients require emergency PCI","confidence":3,"topics":["cardiology"]},{"name":"Conservative management with no angiography, because her risk score is below 6%","confidence":2,"topics":["cardiology"]},{"name":"Elective angiography at 6 months after maximal medical therapy","confidence":2,"topics":["cardiology"]},{"name":"Refer for exercise stress testing before any invasive evaluation","confidence":2,"topics":["cardiology"]}],"reason":"A predicted 6-month mortality above 3.0% places her in the intermediate-or-higher risk band, for which NG185 advises considering coronary angiography with follow-on PCI within 72 hours of first admission when there are no contraindications.
